title: Distributed Message Queue (Kafka-style)
problem: Design a distributed, durable, high-throughput message queue like Apache Kafka.
summary: A partitioned, replicated, append-only log that decouples producers from consumers and guarantees ordering within a partition. The dominant design choice is a partition-leader / in-sync-replica (ISR) replication model: one broker owns each partition for writes, writes are replicated to followers, and a separate controller handles metadata + failover. The main tradeoff is strong per-partition ordering at the cost of cross-partition ordering — and the fact that leader failover causes a brief availability dip (~seconds) for that partition. Sized for ~1M msgs/sec ingest, ~3x fanout to consumers, and 7-day retention.

functional: Producers publish records to named topics; each record lands on exactly one partition
Consumers subscribe in groups; each partition is consumed by exactly one member per group
Strict FIFO ordering within a partition; no global cross-partition ordering guarantee
At-least-once delivery by default, with opt-in idempotent and transactional producers
Configurable retention by time (e.g. 7 days) or size; consumers can replay from any offset
Online topic creation, partition count increase, and broker membership changes without downtime
nonFunctional: Sustain 1M msgs/sec ingest and 3M peak with sub-10ms p99 produce latency
No data loss on single-broker failure (replication factor = 3, min.insync.replicas = 2)
Horizontal scale by adding brokers; no single write bottleneck
Durable on disk with fsync tunable; survives full cluster restart
Leader failover completes in seconds, not minutes

assumptions: Consumer groups: 3x fanout (one message read by 3 independent consumer groups on average)
estimates: Ingest throughput: 1M * 1 KB = 1 GB/s, peak 3 GB/s
Raw storage/day: 1 GB/s * 86400 ≈ 86 TB; x3 replication → 260 TB/day on disk → 1.8 PB for 7-day retention
Read throughput (3x fanout): 3 GB/s steady, 9 GB/s peak
Per broker: 20 GB/s aggregate NIC, ~100 MB/s sustained ingest (260 TB/week / 50 nodes)
Controller metadata: ~1M topic/partition/replica entries → fits comfortably in a single Raft quorum

architecture.mermaid: graph LR producer[Producer Client] --> lb[Load Balancer] lb --> broker[Broker Leader] broker --> log[(Partition Log)] broker --> replica[Replica Broker] ctrl[Controller / ZK] --> broker ctrl --> replica consumer[Consumer Client] --> broker consumer --> coord[Group Coordinator] coord --> offset[(Offset Store)]

producer.name: Producer Client
producer.summary: Application-side library that batches records, selects a partition, and produces to the partition leader.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Resolve topic metadata (leader per partition) on startup + on refresh
- Pick a partition (key hash or round-robin)
- Batch records (linger.ms, batch.size) and compress (lz4/zstd)
- Send PRODUCE request to the partition's leader broker and wait for ack

sections.heading: Acks
sections.body:
- `acks=0` → fire and forget; fastest, can lose data.
- `acks=1` → leader ack only; fast, loses data if leader dies before replication.
- `acks=all` → all in-sync replicas ack; strongest durability, ~2-3x latency.

sections.heading: Idempotence
sections.body: `enable.idempotence=true` attaches a producer id + sequence number so a retry doesn't duplicate a message. Combined with transactions you get exactly-once across a produce-consume-produce cycle.

bottlenecks.title: Accumulator buffer exhaustion under broker slowdown
bottlenecks.trigger: At 1M msgs/sec * 1KB = 1 GB/s ingest, if the partition leader slows (e.g. acks=all waiting on a lagging ISR follower, or leader failover taking ~seconds), in-flight batches pile up. Default buffer.memory=32MB fills in ~30ms at per-producer share of load.
bottlenecks.symptom: producer.send blocks for up to max.block.ms (default 60s), then throws TimeoutException / BufferExhaustedException; application threads stall, upstream request latency spikes, records start being dropped if the app can't backpressure.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Raise buffer.memory to 128-256MB, tune max.block.ms to fail fast (e.g. 5s) and shed load upstream, set reasonable max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5 with idempotence on, and use a bounded async queue in the app so backpressure is explicit rather than hidden in the producer buffer.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on kafka.producer:record-queue-time-avg > 50ms, buffer-available-bytes < 20% of buffer.memory, and waiting-threads > 0 — all exposed via the producer's JMX metrics.

bottlenecks.title: Partition hot-spotting from skewed keys
bottlenecks.trigger: With 1000 partitions across 100 topics (~10 partitions/topic avg) and murmur2(key) % num_partitions routing, a skewed key distribution (e.g. a handful of whale tenants) pins most traffic to 1-2 partitions. A single partition leader caps at ~100 MB/s sustained; a hot partition at 300 MB/s will throttle the whole producer.
bottlenecks.symptom: Uneven broker CPU/NIC usage, producer request-latency-avg climbing for one topic while others are fine, ISR followers for the hot partition falling out of sync, consumer lag concentrated on one partition.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a composite key (tenant_id + random salt) or switch to the built-in UniformStickyPartitioner / custom partitioner that rebalances whales across sub-partitions; increase partition count for hot topics (requires consumer rebalance); for truly extreme skew, route whale tenants to a dedicated topic.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-partition produce rate via kafka.producer:topic.*.partition.*.records-per-sec — alert when max/avg partition rate ratio > 3x; also broker-side BytesInPerSec variance across partitions.

bottlenecks.title: Idempotence + acks=all latency amplification at peak
bottlenecks.trigger: At 3M msgs/sec peak with acks=all + enable.idempotence=true, each PRODUCE must wait for min.insync.replicas=2 ack round-trip (the design notes ~2-3x latency, so 5-15ms end-to-end). With max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5 (required for in-order idempotence), a single producer → leader connection caps at ~5 * (1000/10ms) = 500 batches/sec.
bottlenecks.symptom: Producer throughput plateaus well below NIC capacity; request-latency-avg rises during peak; p99 send latency climbs to 50-100ms under replica lag; CPU on producer app threads is underutilized while send futures queue up.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tune batch.size up (e.g. 256KB-1MB) and linger.ms=5-20ms to amortize the RTT per batch; enable compression.type=zstd or lz4 to reduce replication bytes (already 3 GB/s * 3x replication); shard hot topics across more producer instances (horizontal) rather than one mega-producer; pin min.insync.replicas=2 (not 3) to tolerate one slow follower.
bottlenecks.detection: Track kafka.producer:request-latency-avg, records-per-request-avg, batch-size-avg, and compression-rate-avg; alert if batch-size-avg < 50% of batch.size config (under-batching) or request-latency-p99 > 30ms sustained.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Producer Client exists here For a Kafka-style queue ingesting **1M messages/sec at 1 KB each**, you can't have every application thread open a raw TCP connection and fire one message at a time. The Producer Client is the smart library that sits inside *your* application — it knows which broker leads which partition, batches records together, compresses them, and handles retries when a broker dies. Without this client-side intelligence, the brokers would be hammered with millions of tiny requests and the whole "high-throughput" promise falls apart. ## What happens without it Imagine your app just did `tcp.send(record)` per message. Each 1 KB record becomes its own request with its own round-trip — so at 1M msgs/sec you'd need ~1M requests/sec hitting the broker pool. Brokers burn CPU on request parsing instead of log appends; tail latency explodes; and when a partition leader fails over (a few seconds of unavailability, per the design), your app has no retry logic and starts losing data. The operator sees broker CPU pinned at 100% while actual disk throughput is a tiny fraction of the NIC. ## The number that makes it click At 1M msgs/sec with a typical batch of ~100 records, the producer turns that into **~10,000 PRODUCE requests/sec** across the cluster — a 100× reduction in request count. Spread over 50 brokers that's ~200 req/sec per broker, which is trivial. Compression (lz4/zstd) then shrinks the 1 GB/s wire traffic by 3–5×. ## The trade-off You've pushed real complexity (batching, partition routing, idempotence sequences, retry logic) into every client application — so every language binding has to reimplement it correctly.

lb.name: Bootstrap Load Balancer
lb.summary: L4 LB fronting the broker pool — used only for the initial bootstrap/metadata fetch. Subsequent data traffic goes directly to partition leaders.

sections.heading: Why not LB every request
sections.body: Producers/consumers must talk to the exact broker that leads the partition. An LB in the middle would either randomly route (wrong broker → NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION) or need L7 awareness of topic metadata (overhead). The canonical design uses the LB only for initial broker discovery.

sections.heading: Role
sections.body: Clients configure `bootstrap.servers=kafka-lb:9092`. The first request returns a full metadata map (topic → partition → leader broker) and the client caches it for direct connections afterwards.

bottlenecks.title: Bootstrap thundering herd on cold start / metadata-storm events
bottlenecks.trigger: A cluster-wide event (controller failover, rolling broker restart, network blip) invalidates cached metadata on many clients simultaneously. With ~1M msgs/sec producers plus 3x fanout consumers, there can be tens of thousands of client instances all re-resolving bootstrap.servers at once, slamming the LB with a burst of TCP SYNs and metadata requests far above its 10k steady concurrency budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: Spike in LB connection counts, SYN backlog / TCP listen-overflow drops, clients hang in bootstrap with 'Connection to node -1 could not be established', ingest drops to zero for 10-60s across the cluster even though brokers themselves are healthy.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Front the LB with multiple VIPs and DNS round-robin across all 50 brokers (not a single LB) so bootstrap load spreads; set client reconnect.backoff.ms=500 and reconnect.backoff.max.ms=10000 with jitter; raise LB max concurrent connections to 100k and SYN backlog (net.core.somaxconn) to 32k; consider bypassing the LB entirely by listing several broker hostnames directly in bootstrap.servers.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB new_connections_per_sec > 5x baseline, TCP ListenOverflows / ListenDrops > 0 on LB nodes, and client-side kafka.consumer/producer connection-creation-rate spikes correlated with metadata-age resets.

bottlenecks.title: Stale broker endpoint routing to dead brokers
bottlenecks.trigger: LB health checks run on a 5-30s interval. When a broker in the 50-node pool crashes (see leader-failover op: ~18s detection in ZK, ~1s in KRaft), the LB may still route bootstrap connections to the dead broker for up to one health-check interval.
bottlenecks.symptom: A fraction of new clients fail bootstrap with 'Connection refused' or hang until connect timeout, new deployments or autoscaled consumer pods report intermittent startup failures, existing clients are unaffected because they bypass the LB post-bootstrap.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use aggressive L4 health checks (TCP check on:9092 every 2s, unhealthy after 2 failures); ensure the LB's backend pool is auto-updated from the broker service registry within seconds of a broker going down; clients should list ≥3 bootstrap addresses so one dead endpoint is transparently retried.
bottlenecks.detection: LB backend-health metrics (unhealthy_host_count > 0), spike in LB 5xx/connection-refused counters, alert when broker-down event and LB backend-removal timestamps differ by >10s.

bottlenecks.title: Accidental data-path traffic through the LB
bottlenecks.trigger: Misconfigured clients (missing advertised.listeners on brokers, NAT/k8s networking where broker-returned hostnames aren't reachable, or a client lib that re-resolves bootstrap.servers per request) send PRODUCE/FETCH traffic through the LB instead of going direct-to-leader. At 1 GB/s steady ingest + 3 GB/s fanout reads, even 1% leakage = 40 MB/s of unexpected LB throughput.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB NIC / bandwidth counters climb unexpectedly, elevated LB CPU, NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors at clients when the LB randomly picks a non-leader broker, producer/consumer latency rises from ~5-15ms baseline to 50+ms.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Ensure every broker sets advertised.listeners to its own directly-routable address (not the LB VIP); size the LB for bootstrap-only traffic (few MB/s) and alarm if it exceeds that; block:9092 data-path port on the LB security group except for initial metadata calls if infra allows, or use a dedicated bootstrap-only port.
bottlenecks.detection: LB bytes_in/out > 100 MB/s (should be near-zero for bootstrap-only), broker NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION error rate > 0.1%, correlation of client request-latency-p99 with LB-routed connection share.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a bootstrap LB for a Kafka-style queue In most web systems, a load balancer sits in front of your servers and distributes *every* request. That model breaks here. In a Kafka-style queue, each partition has exactly **one leader broker** that owns writes — if a producer sends a record to the wrong broker, it gets a `NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION` error. So you can't round-robin PRODUCE requests across 50 brokers; the client must talk directly to the specific broker leading the specific partition it's writing to. But clients have to start *somewhere*. When a producer boots up, it doesn't yet know which of the 50 brokers leads which of the 1000 partitions. The bootstrap LB solves exactly this one problem: the client connects to `kafka-lb:9092`, gets a full topic-to-leader map back, caches it, and then opens direct TCP connections to the real brokers. The LB is never in the data path again. ## What happens without it Without a bootstrap endpoint, every client needs a hardcoded list of broker hostnames. When you rotate hardware or add capacity, you'd have to redeploy every producer and consumer. Operators would see deploys stall because some brokers on the old list are gone; developers would see cryptic "connection refused" errors at startup. ## The number At **1 GB/s steady ingest and 3 GB/s fanout reads**, routing all 4 GB/s through an LB would require massive LB capacity and add a hop to every message. By restricting the LB to bootstrap only, it handles maybe a few MB/s of metadata traffic — trivial — while the 4 GB/s flows broker-direct. ## Trade-off Clients become smarter and stateful (they cache and refresh metadata), in exchange for eliminating a bandwidth bottleneck and a wrong-broker routing problem.

broker.name: Broker (Partition Leader)
broker.summary: Stateful Kafka broker process; leads a set of partitions, serves PRODUCE and FETCH, and replicates to followers.

sections.heading: Per-partition state
sections.body:
- Active segment file (log) + index files
- High-watermark (HW): highest offset replicated to all ISR
- Leader epoch, ISR list, controller epoch

sections.heading: Produce path
sections.body:
1. Validate request (auth, ACL, payload size)
2. If leader — append to active segment, update LEO (log-end-offset)
3. Replicate to followers (they pull)
4. Once min.insync.replicas acked, advance HW and ack producer

sections.heading: Fetch path
Why stateful
sections.body: The broker owns the disk that holds its partitions. You can't put partitions behind a stateless tier — the log file is the truth. This shapes everything: sticky ownership, rebalance cost, replica placement.

gained: Stateless brokers — restart without data movement
lost: Extra network hop per write (broker → bookie)
Harder to reason about end-to-end latency

bottlenecks.title: Per-broker NIC saturation from replication + fanout
bottlenecks.trigger: At 1 GB/s steady ingest across 50 brokers, each broker takes ~20 MB/s in but must replicate out to 2 followers (RF=3) AND serve 3x consumer fanout. That's ~20 MB/s in + 40 MB/s replication out + 60 MB/s consumer reads = ~120 MB/s per broker steady, tripling to ~360 MB/s at 3 GB/s peak. A 10 GbE NIC (~1.25 GB/s) headroom evaporates fast when hot partitions concentrate traffic, and the design budget of 20 GB/s aggregate NIC is only achievable with 25/40 GbE.
bottlenecks.symptom: FETCH and PRODUCE request-latency p99 climbing from ~5-15ms to 50-200ms, followers falling out of ISR (replica.lag.time.max.ms breaches), acks=all producers stalling waiting for min.insync.replicas, uneven broker CPU with some NICs pinned at 90%+.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deploy 25 GbE+ NICs on all brokers; enable follower-fetch-from-closest-replica (KIP-392) so cross-AZ consumers don't all hammer the leader; enforce producer compression (zstd/lz4) to shrink the 3x replication traffic; tier cold reads to S3 (KIP-405) so historical replays don't compete with live NIC budget; rack-aware replica placement to keep replication on cheaper intra-rack links.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on node_network_transmit_bytes > 70% NIC capacity sustained, kafka.server:BrokerTopicMetrics.BytesOutPerSec / BytesInPerSec ratio > 5 (indicates fanout amplification), UnderReplicatedPartitions > 0 correlated with NIC utilization, and ISR shrink events per minute.

bottlenecks.title: Page cache thrash from lagging or replay consumers
bottlenecks.trigger: Zero-copy sendfile depends on a 98%+ page cache hit ratio on the active segment tail. With 1.8 PB retained over 7 days and ~36 TB/broker, RAM (~128-256 GB) holds only the last few minutes of data. A single consumer group replaying from offset 0, or a lagging group hours behind, forces disk reads that evict hot pages used by real-time consumers.
bottlenecks.symptom: Real-time consumer FETCH latency jumps from <10ms to 100ms+, broker CPU sys% rises (disk reads no longer zero-copy-friendly), iowait climbs, BytesOutPerSec drops even though consumers are demanding more, specific partitions show consumer lag growing despite adequate headroom.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use separate broker pools (or dedicated fetch quotas via KIP-13 client quotas) for bulk/replay workloads; enable tiered storage (KIP-405) so cold reads go to S3 instead of local disk; set vm.swappiness=1 and vm.dirty_ratio low to protect page cache; isolate noisy consumers with ReplicaAlterLogDirs or move them to read-replicas; alert on lag and throttle replay jobs.
bottlenecks.detection: Track node_memory_Cached, kafka.log:LogFlushStats, kafka.server:BrokerTopicMetrics.TotalFetchRequestsPerSec vs disk read IOPS — a spike in disk reads per fetch signals cache miss. Alert when page-cache-hit-ratio < 95% or when any consumer group lag > 1 hour.

bottlenecks.title: Partition count per broker capping metadata and recovery
bottlenecks.trigger: 1000 partitions * RF=3 = 3000 replicas across 50 brokers = ~60 replicas/broker average, but skewed placement plus hot topics push some brokers to 200+ replicas. Each partition costs file handles (log + 2 indexes * N segments), a fetcher thread slot, and controller metadata churn. Broker startup log recovery is serial per log dir and takes ~1s per 1000 segments, so a broker with 200 partitions * 7 segments = 1400 segments means ~1-2 min recovery after an unclean shutdown.
bottlenecks.symptom: Slow broker startup (minutes instead of seconds), prolonged UnderReplicatedPartitions window after rolling restarts, file-descriptor exhaustion errors in broker logs, controller's LeaderAndIsrRequest fan-out stalling during failover, num.recovery.threads.per.data.dir bottleneck on restart.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Raise num.recovery.threads.per.data.dir to 8+; use multiple log.dirs on separate SSDs for parallel recovery; raise ulimit -n to 1M; cap segment count by tuning segment.bytes (1GB) and segment.ms; avoid over-partitioning topics — aim for <4000 partitions per broker (Kafka's soft limit); enable clean-shutdown hooks so the controlled-shutdown path skips full recovery.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor kafka.server:ReplicaManager.PartitionCount per broker, kafka.log:LogManager startup duration, open file descriptors (process_open_fds / ulimit), and post-restart time-to-ISR-restored — alert if recovery > 60s or partition count > 4000 per broker.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a partition leader exists here For a Kafka-style queue ingesting **1M messages/sec**, you need one authoritative place that decides the order of writes for each partition. That's the broker's job as *leader*: it owns a slice of partitions on its local disk, accepts every PRODUCE for those partitions, assigns each record a monotonically increasing offset, and replicates to followers. Ordering inside a partition is one of the few strong guarantees the whole system makes — and it only works because exactly one broker at a time is allowed to append. No leader means no agreed-upon order. ## What happens without it Imagine two brokers both accept writes for the same partition. Producer A sends "order placed," Producer B sends "order cancelled" a millisecond later — but the two brokers disagree on which came first, and their logs diverge. Consumers on different replicas see different histories. The operator sees silent data corruption; the user sees an order that's both cancelled and active. You'd need a consensus protocol on *every single write* to fix this, which destroys throughput. ## The number At 1 GB/s ingest spread across **50 brokers**, each broker averages ~20 MB/s of writes, and with 1000 partitions that's ~20 partitions per broker leading writes. Because appends are sequential per partition and use the OS page cache with zero-copy `sendfile` on the read side, a single broker comfortably sustains ~100 MB/s — 5× headroom over steady load, enough to absorb the 3× peak. ## Trade-off Sticky leadership means a crashed broker causes a brief (~seconds) availability gap for its partitions until the controller elects a new leader.

log.name: Partition Log (on-disk)
log.summary: Append-only segmented log files on local SSD. The physical representation of a partition.

sections.heading: Segment layout
sections.body:
```
/data/kafka/orders-0/ 00000000000012000000.log # records 00000000000012000000.index # offset → byte position 00000000000012000000.timeindex # timestamp → offset 00000000000012512341.log # next segment (rolls at 1GB or 7d)
```

sections.heading: Why segmented
sections.body: Old segments can be deleted or tiered to S3 without touching the active segment. Indexes are sparse — every 4KB of log, not every record — so they stay small and cache-hot.

sections.heading: Zero-copy reads
sections.body: FETCH responses use `sendfile(2)` to copy bytes directly from page cache to socket, bypassing user space. A single broker serves 1 GB/s of reads with ~10% CPU because of this.

bottlenecks.title: Sustained write IOPS + replication amplification saturating SSD
bottlenecks.trigger: Each broker absorbs ~20 MB/s of producer ingest at 1 GB/s steady, but because it also hosts follower replicas for other brokers' partitions (RF=3), the actual disk write load is ~60 MB/s per broker steady and ~180 MB/s at 3 GB/s peak. Add periodic fsync, index writes every 4KB, and log-compaction rewrites of __consumer_offsets, and a single SATA SSD (~500 MB/s, ~80k IOPS) starts queuing under peak bursts, especially with many partitions fsync'ing concurrently.
bottlenecks.symptom: Rising iowait on the broker, PRODUCE request-latency-p99 climbing from ~5ms to 50-200ms, LogFlushRateAndTimeMs spiking, followers falling behind and triggering ISR shrink, producers with acks=all stalling intermittently.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use NVMe SSDs (≥1 GB/s sustained write, 500k+ IOPS) with multiple log.dirs striped across devices for parallelism; keep flush.messages / flush.ms at defaults (rely on replication, not fsync, for durability); separate __consumer_offsets onto its own disk; set segment.bytes=1GB to minimize segment-roll overhead; ensure XFS with noatime mount options.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on node_disk_io_time_seconds_total utilization > 70%, kafka.log:LogFlushStats.LogFlushRateAndTimeMs p99 > 500ms, and disk write queue depth > 32 sustained; correlate with UnderReplicatedPartitions > 0.

bottlenecks.title: Segment/index file-descriptor and mmap exhaustion
bottlenecks.trigger: Each partition has N segments * 3 files (.log,.index,.timeindex). With 1.8 PB / 7 days retention and segment.bytes=1GB, that's ~1.8M segments cluster-wide, or ~36,000 segments per broker => ~108,000 open file descriptors + mmap regions per broker for indexes alone. Default ulimit -n = 1024 is 100x too low; even typical 65k limits can be breached on brokers carrying skewed partition counts (200+ replicas).
bottlenecks.symptom: Broker logs 'Too many open files' errors, segment rolls fail, new topic/partition creation fails with IOException, producer and consumer requests error out with unrelated-looking failures, broker may crash on next log roll.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Set ulimit -n to 1,000,000 on broker hosts; raise vm.max_map_count to 262144+; tune segment.bytes up (e.g. 2GB) or segment.ms longer to reduce segment count on low-throughput partitions; tier old segments to S3 via KIP-405 so local FD count reflects hot data only; monitor per-broker partition count and cap at ~4000.
bottlenecks.detection: Track process_open_fds / process_max_fds ratio — alert at >70%; monitor kafka.log:LogManager.NumLogSegments per broker and vm.max_map_count utilization via /proc/<pid>/maps line count.

bottlenecks.title: Retention deletion bursts stalling the active write path
bottlenecks.trigger: With 7-day retention on 36 TB/broker, segments age out continuously; log.retention.check.interval.ms (default 5min) triggers a scan that can delete hundreds of 1GB segment files at once across many partitions. A bulk unlink on XFS/ext4 for GB-sized files can block the filesystem journal for seconds, and old page-cache pages get evicted, disrupting zero-copy FETCH for real-time consumers.
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic latency spikes every ~5 minutes visible in PRODUCE and FETCH p99, brief drops in BytesOutPerSec, kernel iowait bursts, consumer lag oscillating, page-cache-hit-ratio dipping right after retention sweeps.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Stagger retention by using log.retention.check.interval.ms=30000 with smaller per-tick deletion counts; prefer tiered storage (KIP-405) so deletion = S3 metadata op, not local unlink; use XFS (faster large-file deletes than ext4); ensure async deletion is enabled (file.delete.delay.ms default 60s already helps); avoid giant segment.bytes that amplify per-file deletion cost.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on periodic iowait spikes aligned with log.retention.check.interval.ms; track kafka.log:LogManager.OfflineLogDirectoryCount and kafka.server:BrokerTopicMetrics.BytesRejectedPerSec; watch for correlation between request-latency-p99 peaks and retention-sweep log lines.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why an append-only log on disk, for this queue A Kafka-style queue promises **durability** (messages survive broker crashes) and **replayability** (a new consumer can read last Tuesday's events). Both require writing messages to disk — but *how* you write matters enormously at 1 GB/s ingest. The partition log is literally just a file that you append to, forever, in order. No updates, no deletes of individual records, no B-tree index to maintain. That simplicity is the whole point: sequential writes to an SSD are 10-100× faster than random writes, and the OS page cache naturally keeps the "tail" of the log hot in RAM, so recent reads (the 99% case) never touch disk at all. ## What happens without it Imagine the broker stored messages in a traditional database table instead. Every PRODUCE becomes an INSERT with index updates; every FETCH becomes a range query. At 1 GB/s you'd shred any OLTP database within minutes — the operator sees disk IOPS pinned and query latency climbing into seconds, the user sees producer timeouts, and consumers fall hours behind because random-read FETCHes can't keep up with sequential-write ingest. ## The number The design retains **1.8 PB over 7 days** (86 TB/day × 3 replicas × 7). Spread across 50 brokers, that's ~36 TB per broker. No database indexes that volume cheaply — but a segmented log with *sparse* indexes (one entry per 4 KB) keeps the index under ~10 GB per broker, small enough to stay in RAM. FETCH becomes: binary-search the index, `sendfile` the bytes from page cache to socket. That's how one broker sustains ~100 MB/s reads at ~10% CPU. ## The trade-off You give up the ability to update or delete individual messages — the log is immutable until a whole segment ages out.

replica.name: Replica Broker (Follower)
replica.summary: Follower brokers that pull records from the leader and maintain an in-sync replica (ISR) of each partition.

sections.heading: Pull-based replication
sections.body: Followers issue FETCH requests to the leader (same API as consumers). The leader tracks which followers are caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms → those form the ISR.

sections.heading: Why pull, not push
sections.body: Pull lets the leader natively apply backpressure: a slow follower just FETCHes slower. A push model requires per-follower flow control in the leader — more complex.

sections.heading: Out-of-ISR
sections.body: Follower falls behind > replica.lag.time.max.ms → removed from ISR. Produces with acks=all no longer wait on it. When it catches up, it rejoins and begins counting toward acks again.

bottlenecks.title: Follower fetch NIC saturation from replication fan-in
bottlenecks.trigger: Every follower must pull the full write stream of each partition it replicates. At 1 GB/s cluster ingest with RF=3, each broker averages ~40 MB/s of inbound replication traffic (2x its own ~20 MB/s lead share) and triples to ~120 MB/s at 3 GB/s peak. Hot-partition skew or cross-AZ placement can push a single follower's fetch pipe to 300+ MB/s — well beyond a 10 GbE budget when combined with its own PRODUCE/FETCH duties.
bottlenecks.symptom: replica.lag.time.max.ms breaches, ISR shrink events, acks=all producers stalling waiting for min.insync.replicas, UnderReplicatedPartitions > 0, fetcher threads pegged, cross-AZ egress bill spiking.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deploy 25 GbE+ NICs; enforce producer-side compression (zstd/lz4) so replication bytes shrink 3-5x; use rack-aware replica placement (broker.rack) to keep replication intra-rack where possible; raise num.replica.fetchers from 1 to 4-8 so fan-in parallelizes across sockets; set replica.fetch.response.max.bytes ≥ 10MB to amortize RTT.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on kafka.server:ReplicaFetcherManager.MaxLag > 10000, UnderReplicatedPartitions > 0 for >60s, kafka.server:FetcherLagMetrics per-partition lag trending up, and node_network_receive_bytes > 70% NIC capacity on follower brokers.

bottlenecks.title: ISR churn from transient follower slowness
bottlenecks.trigger: With replica.lag.time.max.ms default 30s and 143-record batches arriving at sub-ms cadence, a single follower GC pause, disk fsync stall, or network microburst can push its LEO >30s behind. At 1000 partitions × RF=3 = 3000 replicas, even a 0.1% per-minute flap rate means ~3 ISR shrink/expand events per minute cluster-wide, each triggering controller metadata fan-out and acks=all producer stalls.
bottlenecks.symptom: Oscillating ISR membership in controller logs, periodic PRODUCE latency spikes to 100s of ms on acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2 occasionally breached forcing NotEnoughReplicasException, consumer lag bouncing as HW advancement stutters.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tune replica.lag.time.max.ms to 10s for faster detection of truly dead followers but with replica.fetch.wait.max.ms=500 to avoid false positives; use G1GC or ZGC with MaxGCPauseMillis=50 on follower JVMs; isolate __consumer_offsets and high-traffic partitions onto separate log.dirs; set min.insync.replicas=2 with RF=3 so one slow follower doesn't block acks.
bottlenecks.detection: Track kafka.server:ReplicaManager.IsrShrinksPerSec and IsrExpandsPerSec — alert if either > 1/sec sustained; monitor kafka.server:FetcherLagMetrics.ConsumerLag per follower-partition and GC pause time > 200ms on broker JVMs.

bottlenecks.title: Truncation + catch-up storm after follower restart
bottlenecks.trigger: When a follower restarts (rolling upgrade, crash, or post-leader-failover rejoin as in the failover op), it must truncate to the last known safe HW then re-fetch everything produced during its absence. At 20 MB/s per-partition write rate and 10-min downtime, that's ~12 GB to re-replicate per partition; a broker hosting ~60 replicas faces ~700 GB of catch-up reads hitting live leaders, competing with real-time traffic.
bottlenecks.symptom: Rejoining broker shows high sustained inbound traffic for minutes, leaders it's fetching from see elevated FETCH load and page-cache eviction of the hot tail, real-time consumer p99 latency rises, UnderReplicatedPartitions stays > 0 long after the broker process is 'up', preferred-replica election delayed.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable tiered storage (KIP-405) so catch-up reads hit S3 not leader SSDs; set replica.fetch.max.bytes=10MB and num.replica.fetchers=8 to parallelize catch-up; use controlled shutdown (controlled.shutdown.enable=true) so partitions migrate before restart avoiding truncation; throttle recovery with leader.replication.throttled.rate to protect live traffic; stagger rolling restarts with long wait-for-ISR gates.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on kafka.server:ReplicaFetcherManager.MaxLag > 1M messages after a broker rejoin, UnderReplicatedPartitions remaining > 0 for >5min post-startup, and correlation of leader-side FETCH BytesOutPerSec spikes with follower rejoin events.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why follower replicas exist in this queue The whole point of a Kafka-style queue is that once a producer gets an ack, the message **will not be lost** — even if a broker's disk dies or the machine catches fire. But each partition has exactly one leader broker that owns writes, and that leader's SSD is a single point of failure. Follower replicas solve this: each partition is copied onto 2 other brokers (replication factor 3), so if the leader dies, a follower already has every byte and can take over. Followers are also what makes the `acks=all` durability guarantee real — the leader waits for followers to confirm before telling the producer "it's safe." ## What happens without followers With RF=1, a single disk failure permanently loses every message on that broker's partitions. The user sees orders silently vanish; the operator sees a 36 TB hole (that's one broker's share of the 1.8 PB retention) with no way to recover. Worse, during the leader's ~18s failover window, there'd be no surviving copy to promote — the partition would be offline until someone restored from backup, if a backup even existed. Consumers downstream would either block or skip ahead, breaking ordering. ## The number At **1 GB/s ingest × 3× replication = 3 GB/s** of total write traffic, spread across 50 brokers, each broker absorbs ~60 MB/s of follower fetch traffic on top of its own ~20 MB/s of leader writes. That's why the design budgets 20 GB/s aggregate NIC — replication isn't free, it's literally 2/3 of the bytes moving through the cluster. ## The trade-off You pay 3× storage and 3× network to survive any single broker failure without data loss.

ctrl.name: Controller / Metadata Quorum (Raft / ZooKeeper)
ctrl.summary: Single active controller that owns cluster metadata and performs leader elections on failover.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Maintain topic → partition → (leader, replicas, ISR) map
- Watch for broker liveness (heartbeat)
- On broker failure, elect a new leader for each affected partition from the ISR
- Propagate metadata updates to all brokers (LeaderAndIsr, UpdateMetadata)

sections.heading: Raft vs ZooKeeper
sections.body: Original Kafka stored metadata in ZooKeeper (external ensemble). Since KIP-500 (KRaft mode), Kafka embeds its own Raft quorum — no external dep, faster controller failover.

sections.heading: Scale
sections.body: A single controller can manage ~1M partitions; metadata deltas are small (<100 bytes per partition state change).

lost: Metadata operations bottleneck at million-partition scale

bottlenecks.title: Metadata fan-out storm on broker failure
bottlenecks.trigger: When a broker fails holding ~60 partition leaderships (3000 replicas / 50 brokers), the controller must compute new leaders for each affected partition and send LeaderAndIsrRequest + UpdateMetadataRequest to all 49 surviving brokers. That's ~60 partition state changes × 50 brokers = ~3000 RPCs in a burst, plus a full metadata map push (~1M partition entries) to every broker. During rolling restarts or correlated rack failures, multiple brokers fail in quick succession and the fan-out compounds.
bottlenecks.symptom: Controller CPU spikes to 100% for 5-30s after a broker failure, LeaderAndIsr requests queue up, affected partitions show NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors for longer than the expected ~1s (KRaft) / ~18s (ZK) failover budget, producer/consumer p99 latency jumps cluster-wide even for partitions on healthy brokers, controller-to-broker request queue depth climbs.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use KRaft (KIP-500) instead of ZooKeeper — incremental metadata deltas via Raft log replication replace full UpdateMetadataRequest snapshots, cutting fan-out bytes by 100x+; tune controller.quorum.request.timeout.ms and set controller.quota.window.num to rate-limit fan-out; keep partition count per broker < 4000 so per-failure work stays bounded; use rack-aware placement so a rack loss doesn't dump 10+ brokers' worth of leadership recomputation on the controller at once.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on kafka.controller:ControllerEventManager.EventQueueSize > 100, ControllerEventManager.EventQueueTimeMs p99 > 1s, LeaderElectionRateAndTimeMs spiking, and time-to-restore-leadership (from broker-down event to all affected partitions having a leader) > 5s in KRaft or > 30s in ZK.

bottlenecks.title: Single active controller write bottleneck on metadata churn
bottlenecks.trigger: Only one controller is active at a time; all metadata writes (ISR shrinks/expands, leader elections, topic creates, partition reassignments) serialize through its Raft log. At 1000 partitions × RF=3 = 3000 replicas with typical ISR flap rates of 1-5/sec during load spikes (see replica pre-build), plus preferred-leader-election cron jobs and ongoing partition reassignments for rebalancing, the controller can see 100s-1000s of metadata ops/sec. Raft commit requires quorum fsync across 3-5 controller nodes, capping throughput at ~5-10k ops/sec on NVMe.
bottlenecks.symptom: ISR changes take seconds to propagate, acks=all producers stall waiting for HW advancement because ISR updates lag, CreateTopics / AlterPartitionReassignments API calls time out, controller log (@metadata topic in KRaft) grows rapidly, follower controllers fall behind on Raft replication.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deploy dedicated controller nodes (not co-located with brokers) on NVMe with fsync < 1ms; keep Raft quorum at 3 (not 5) unless geo-spread is required — smaller quorums commit faster; batch ISR updates via AlterPartitionReassignments KIP-497 style incremental APIs; throttle bulk admin operations (topic creation, reassignments) with request quotas; avoid running preferred-leader-election auto-rebalance during peak traffic windows.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor kafka.controller:KafkaController.ActiveControllerCount == 1 always, controller-side MetadataLogProcessing latency p99 > 100ms, @metadata topic produce rate, and kafka.server:RaftManager.CommitLatencyMs p99 > 50ms; alert on AlterIsr request rate > 500/sec sustained.

bottlenecks.title: Slow ZooKeeper failover vs KRaft on controller death
bottlenecks.trigger: If running the legacy ZooKeeper-backed controller (alternative listed in the design), controller failover involves ZK session timeout (default 18s) + new controller reading the entire metadata state from ZK (~1M partitions × ~100 bytes = ~100 MB of znodes, read serially at ~1000 znodes/sec = 15-30s). Total controller unavailability can reach 30-60s during which no leader elections or metadata updates complete.
bottlenecks.symptom: During controller death, any concurrent broker failure leaves partitions leaderless for the full failover window — producers see NOT_CONTROLLER / NOT_LEADER for 30-60s, consumer lag spikes, operator dashboards show ActiveControllerCount = 0, cluster-wide admin operations hang.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Migrate to KRaft mode (KIP-500) which cuts failover to ~1s because the Raft quorum already has the full metadata log in memory — no cold read from ZK required; if stuck on ZK, tune zookeeper.session.timeout.ms down to 6s with faster tickTime and ensure ZK ensemble is on dedicated hardware with low-latency disks; pre-load metadata caches on standby controllers.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on ActiveControllerCount!= 1 for > 5s, kafka.controller:ControllerChangeRateAndTimeMs (time to become active) > 10s, and track ZK session expiration events in controller logs; measure end-to-end failover by injecting controlled controller restarts and timing metadata availability.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Controller exists in this queue This queue has **50 brokers**, **1000 partitions**, and a rule that each partition has exactly one leader at any moment. Somebody has to be the authoritative source of truth for "who leads what" — otherwise two brokers might both think they lead `orders-7`, accept writes independently, and corrupt the log. The controller is that single source of truth. It holds the topic → partition → (leader, replicas, ISR) map, watches broker heartbeats, and when a broker dies it picks a new leader from the surviving in-sync replicas and tells everyone about the change. ## What happens without it Without a controller, imagine broker-12 (leading 60 partitions) crashes. There's no one to notice, no one to elect replacements, and no one to tell the other 49 brokers "stop fetching from broker-12, fetch from broker-27 now." Producers keep sending to a dead address and get connection errors forever; consumers stall; the 180 partitions on broker-12's replicas (as leader or follower) are effectively offline. The operator sees the cluster permanently stuck after any single failure — which defeats the entire purpose of RF=3. ## The number The controller manages **~1M partition/replica metadata entries** (1000 partitions × 3 replicas, with room to grow). Each state change is under 100 bytes, so the full metadata fits comfortably in a single Raft quorum's memory. That's why one active controller suffices — this isn't a throughput problem, it's a coordination problem, and coordination traffic is tiny compared to the 1 GB/s data path. ## The trade-off Centralizing metadata means controller failover itself becomes a cluster-wide event (~1s in KRaft, ~18s in ZooKeeper) — a brief window where no new leader elections can happen.

consumer.name: Consumer Client
consumer.summary: Application-side library that joins a consumer group and pulls records from assigned partitions.

sections.heading: Poll loop
sections.body:
```
consumer.subscribe(["orders"])
while True: records = consumer.poll(timeout=100ms) for r in records: process(r) consumer.commitSync # move offset forward
```

sections.heading: Group semantics
sections.body: Consumers in the same `group.id` share partitions (one partition → one consumer in the group). Changing group size triggers a rebalance.

sections.heading: Offset commits
sections.body: Auto-commit every 5s or manual. Manual is safer: you commit only after processing. Offsets are stored in the internal `__consumer_offsets` topic.

bottlenecks.title: Stop-the-world rebalance storms on group membership changes
bottlenecks.trigger: With 1000 partitions, 3x fanout (so ~3 consumer groups totalling potentially hundreds of consumer instances per group for the 3 GB/s steady / 9 GB/s peak read load), any consumer pod restart, deploy, autoscale event, or missed heartbeat (session.timeout.ms default 10s) triggers a JoinGroup → SyncGroup cycle. Under the eager (non-cooperative) protocol, every consumer in the group revokes ALL its partitions and reassigns from scratch — a group of 100 consumers churning over 300+ partitions can take 10-60s to complete.
bottlenecks.symptom: Consumer lag spikes by millions of messages during deploys, poll returns no records for tens of seconds, downstream processing latency breaches SLO, CommitFailedException on offset commits during revoke, cascading rebalances if processing-time > max.poll.interval.ms (default 5min) causes members to be kicked out mid-batch.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Switch partition.assignment.strategy to CooperativeStickyAssignor (KIP-429) so only impacted partitions move; set session.timeout.ms=45s and heartbeat.interval.ms=3s to tolerate brief GC pauses; tune max.poll.records down (e.g. 100-500) and max.poll.interval.ms up so slow processing doesn't kick members; use static group membership (group.instance.id) so pod restarts within session.timeout don't trigger rebalance at all.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on kafka.consumer:coordinator-metrics.rebalance-rate-per-hour > 2, rebalance-latency-avg > 5s, failed-rebalance-total > 0; track records-lag-max spikes correlated with JoinGroup log lines; monitor heartbeat-response-time-max p99.

bottlenecks.title: Consumer lag from processing throughput below fetch throughput
bottlenecks.trigger: Each partition delivers up to ~20 MB/s of records (1 GB/s / ~50 leader-partitions per broker share). If the application's per-record handler takes >1ms (DB write, downstream RPC, JSON parse on a 1KB payload), a single-threaded poll loop tops out at ~1000 records/sec = 1 MB/s — 20x slower than ingest. At 3x fanout and 3 GB/s steady reads, any group processing slower than produce rate accumulates lag linearly.
bottlenecks.symptom: records-lag-max climbs monotonically, consumer never catches up, real-time SLOs missed, page-cache misses on broker side (lag consumer reads cold segments from disk evicting hot pages for real-time consumers — see broker pre-build #2), eventually hitting 7-day retention and losing records permanently.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Scale consumer group size up to partition count (one consumer per partition is the max parallelism — beyond that you need more partitions); offload handler work to a bounded worker thread pool while keeping poll fast (careful: breaks ordering unless keyed); use batch processing (handle(records) not handle(record)) to amortize per-call overhead; increase fetch.min.bytes and fetch.max.wait.ms to get fuller batches; pre-provision partition count (e.g. 2-4x consumer count) to allow horizontal headroom without re-partitioning.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on kafka.consumer:fetch-manager-metrics.records-lag-max > 100k per partition, records-consumed-rate < records-produced-rate for same topic sustained > 5min, time-lag via __consumer_offsets vs wall clock > 60s; track poll-latency-avg and process-time-per-record.

bottlenecks.title: Offset commit semantics causing duplicate processing or data loss
bottlenecks.trigger: With auto-commit (enable.auto.commit=true, auto.commit.interval.ms=5s default), offsets advance before records are fully processed. A consumer crash between commit and processing re-delivers up to 5s of records (at 20 MB/s that's ~100 MB / ~100k records per partition). Conversely, committing after processing with at-least-once semantics double-delivers on retry. At 1M msgs/sec * 3x fanout = 3M consumes/sec, even a 0.01% failure rate yields 300 duplicates/sec cluster-wide.
bottlenecks.symptom: Downstream side effects happen twice (duplicate emails, double-charged orders, idempotency-violation errors in databases), or missing records reported by business reconciliation jobs; inconsistent behavior between graceful shutdown and crash scenarios; intermittent alerts from downstream dedup systems.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Disable auto-commit (enable.auto.commit=false), commitSync only after side effects are durable; make handlers idempotent (unique message_id + dedup table, or UPSERT semantics); for exactly-once, use Kafka transactions with isolation.level=read_committed and the transactional producer — ties consume-process-produce into one atomic commit; pair with transactional.id for producer fencing across restarts.
bottlenecks.detection: Track duplicate detection counters in downstream systems, alert on commit-latency-avg p99 > 500ms (signals commits blocking processing), monitor kafka.consumer:consumer-coordinator-metrics.commit-rate and failed-commit-total; add business-level reconciliation checks comparing produced vs processed record counts.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Consumer Client exists here For a Kafka-style queue serving **3 GB/s of fanout reads to three independent consumer groups**, the broker can't be in charge of tracking who has read what. If it were, it would need to remember the read position of every consumer across every partition — and worse, push records to them at whatever pace each one could handle. The Consumer Client flips this around: *the consumer* tells the broker "give me records starting at offset X," processes them, and commits its own progress. The broker just serves byte ranges from a log, which is exactly what makes the 1 GB/s steady ingest sustainable. ## What happens without it Imagine consumers just opened a raw socket and asked for "the next message." The broker would have to track per-consumer cursors, buffer undelivered records, and handle slow consumers by either dropping data or running out of memory. One stuck consumer (say, a downstream database hiccup) would start eating broker RAM; operators would see brokers OOM-kill themselves; producers would back up because the broker is busy babysitting readers instead of appending writes. Ordering guarantees would also collapse — without a single consumer per partition per group, two threads could process the same partition out of order. ## The number With **3× fanout on 1 GB/s ingest = 3 GB/s of reads**, spread across 1000 partitions, each partition delivers ~3 MB/s to each consumer group. Pull-based polling lets each consumer fetch batches (~1 MB at a time = ~3 fetches/sec/partition) instead of the broker pushing millions of tiny messages. Backpressure is automatic: a slow consumer just polls less often, and lag shows up as a number on a dashboard rather than a broker crash. ## Trade-off Consumers become responsible for their own progress tracking and failure recovery — a slow or buggy consumer silently accumulates lag until someone notices.

coord.name: Group Coordinator
coord.summary: One broker per consumer group elected as coordinator; manages membership, heartbeats, and partition assignment.

sections.heading: Election
sections.body: Coordinator for group `g` = broker that leads partition `hash(g) % 50` of `__consumer_offsets`. This means the coordinator is colocated with the group's offset storage — no extra hop.

sections.heading: Rebalance protocol
sections.body:
1. Consumer sends JoinGroup → coordinator buffers members
2. Coordinator picks a leader consumer, gives it the member list
3. Leader runs the assignor (RangeAssignor / RoundRobin / Sticky) and returns the assignment
4. SyncGroup distributes assignments back to each member

sections.heading: Incremental rebalance
sections.body: Newer protocol (Cooperative Sticky) only moves a small subset of partitions during scale events, avoiding stop-the-world rebalance. Critical for multi-thousand-partition deployments.

bottlenecks.title: Rebalance storm from large group membership changes
bottlenecks.trigger: At 3 GB/s steady read fanout across 3 consumer groups, each group may have 100+ consumer instances (one per partition for max parallelism on 1000 partitions). A single pod restart, deploy, or missed heartbeat (session.timeout.ms=10s default) triggers JoinGroup+SyncGroup; with eager RangeAssignor, all members revoke all partitions. Under rolling deploys or autoscale bursts, the coordinator can see 10+ rebalances/min per group, each coordinating state across 100s of members and 1000s of partition assignments.
bottlenecks.symptom: Consumer poll returns empty for 10-60s during rebalance, records-lag-max spikes by millions, coordinator broker CPU pegged handling JoinGroup state machines, CommitFailedException on in-flight offset commits, cascading rebalances if processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms, cluster-wide consumer throughput drops even on unaffected groups sharing the coordinator broker.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce partition.assignment.strategy=CooperativeStickyAssignor (KIP-429) so only moved partitions rebalance; use static group membership (group.instance.id) to skip rebalance on pod restart within session.timeout.ms; raise session.timeout.ms=45s with heartbeat.interval.ms=3s; cap consumer group size at partition count; spread groups across coordinator brokers by tuning __consumer_offsets partition count (default 50) upward to 200+ so coordinator load distributes.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on kafka.coordinator.group:GroupMetadataManager.NumGroups per broker imbalance >2x, rebalance-rate-per-hour >5 per group, rebalance-latency-avg >5s, JoinGroup request-queue-size >100, and coordinator-broker CPU spikes correlated with deploy events.

bottlenecks.title: Coordinator hotspotting from skewed group-to-partition hashing
bottlenecks.trigger: Coordinator for group g = broker leading hash(g) % 50 of __consumer_offsets. With only ~3 consumer groups at 3x fanout but potentially dozens of sub-groups (microservices, replay jobs, analytics pipelines), the hash distribution across 50 __consumer_offsets partitions is coarse. One broker can end up coordinating the largest group (100+ members, highest commit rate) plus several others, while peers coordinate idle groups. At 1M msgs/sec consumed * 3x = 3M commits/sec cluster-wide if committing per-record, even at batched commits (every 100 records) that's 30k commits/sec concentrated on a few coordinators.
bottlenecks.symptom: One or two brokers show elevated OFFSET_COMMIT request latency (p99 >100ms vs <10ms baseline), heartbeat responses delayed causing false session timeouts and rebalance cascades, __consumer_offsets partitions on hot brokers falling behind in replication, uneven broker CPU with coordinator brokers pegged while others idle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Increase offsets.topic.num.partitions from 50 to 200+ at cluster init (immutable after creation) to smooth hash distribution; rename problematic groups to rehash onto cooler partitions; isolate __consumer_offsets onto dedicated log.dirs on NVMe to absorb commit write amplification; use admin-driven preferred-leader-election to rebalance __consumer_offsets leadership across all 50 brokers evenly.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor kafka.coordinator.group:GroupMetadataManager.NumOffsets and NumGroups per broker — alert if any broker >3x the cluster median; track OFFSET_COMMIT request-latency p99 per broker and BytesInPerSec on __consumer_offsets partitions; watch for heartbeat-response-time-max spikes correlated to specific coordinator brokers.

bottlenecks.title: Coordinator failover stalling consumer progress on broker death
bottlenecks.trigger: When the coordinator broker for a group dies (see leader-failover op: ~18s in ZK-mode, ~1s in KRaft), all groups it coordinated lose their heartbeat endpoint. At 50 __consumer_offsets partitions / 50 brokers = ~1 partition per broker, each broker coordinates ~6% of groups; losing one broker orphans dozens of consumer groups simultaneously. Consumers must FindCoordinator again, the new coordinator must load group state from __consumer_offsets (reading compacted log up to offsets.load.buffer.size), which for a large group with 100 members and millions of committed offsets takes seconds to tens of seconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: All consumers in affected groups see CoordinatorNotAvailableException, heartbeats fail, offset commits error out, poll stalls until new coordinator finishes loading, lag spikes across many unrelated groups simultaneously during a single broker failure, 'Loading group metadata' log lines on the new coordinator for 10-30s.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use KRaft mode for faster metadata convergence after failover; tune offsets.load.buffer.size to 16MB+ so group state loads in fewer passes; reduce __consumer_offsets segment.bytes to 100MB and enable aggressive log compaction (min.cleanable.dirty.ratio=0.1) so loading reads less data; place __consumer_offsets on NVMe; ensure RF=3 with min.insync.replicas=2 on __consumer_offsets so failover always has a warm replica; pre-warm by keeping offsets.retention.minutes reasonable (default 7 days may bloat state).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on kafka.coordinator.group:GroupMetadataManager.group-load-time-max >5s, FindCoordinator error rate >0/sec sustained, CoordinatorNotAvailable errors in consumer logs, and time-from-broker-down-event to all-groups-reloaded >10s measured via synthetic consumers.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Group Coordinator exists for this queue For a Kafka-style queue with **1000 partitions** and **3× consumer fanout**, each consumer group (say, "order-processor", "fraud-checker", "analytics-loader") needs to spread those 1000 partitions across its worker pods. Someone has to decide *which consumer owns which partition*, notice when a consumer dies, and reassign its partitions elsewhere — all without two consumers ever reading the same partition at the same time (which would break ordering and cause duplicate processing). The Group Coordinator is that someone. It's not a separate service — it's just one broker per group, chosen by hashing the group name, that runs the membership protocol and stores the group's committed offsets right next to it. ## What happens without it Imagine 100 consumer pods in a group with no coordinator. Two pods both claim partition `orders-7` and process the same records, so downstream databases get double-writes. A pod crashes and nobody reassigns its 10 partitions — those partitions just stop being read, lag climbs by millions of messages, and the operator's dashboard shows a growing backlog with no obvious cause. Meanwhile every pod is independently asking "where did I leave off?" with no agreed-upon answer. ## The number At **3 GB/s of fanout reads** across 1000 partitions, a single group might run ~100 consumer pods (one per ~10 partitions). Colocating the coordinator with the group's offset-storage partition means a commit is *one* local append — no cross-broker hop — so even at tens of thousands of commits/sec per group, it stays cheap. ## Trade-off Coordinator death stalls the whole group for a few seconds until a new broker takes over.

offset.name: Offset Store (__consumer_offsets topic)
offset.summary: Kafka's internal compacted topic storing (group, topic, partition) → committed_offset.

sections.heading: Compacted topic
sections.body: Log compaction retains only the latest value per key → perfect for offsets where old commits are obsolete. 50 partitions by default — groups are hashed to partitions for parallelism.

sections.heading: Why a topic, not a DB
sections.body: Reusing the broker's own storage primitive means no external dependency (originally it was ZooKeeper; moving to a topic scaled to millions of commits/sec). Each group's commits land on the same partition → same coordinator → atomic.

sections.heading: Read on startup
sections.body: When a consumer joins, it fetches its committed offset from the coordinator (one __consumer_offsets read) and starts from there.

bottlenecks.title: Commit write amplification overwhelming __consumer_offsets partitions
bottlenecks.trigger: At 1M msgs/sec consumed × 3x fanout = 3M records/sec read cluster-wide across ~3 consumer groups. Even with batched commits every 100 records (or 5s auto-commit), that's ~30k commits/sec distributed over only 50 __consumer_offsets partitions = ~600 commits/sec/partition. With RF=3 on __consumer_offsets, each commit triggers replication fanout. Skewed group-to-partition hashing can concentrate 5-10k commits/sec onto a single partition.
bottlenecks.symptom: OFFSET_COMMIT request-latency p99 climbs from <10ms baseline to 100-500ms, consumer commitSync calls block and stall poll loops (adding to consumer lag), __consumer_offsets partitions fall behind in replication triggering ISR shrink, hot coordinator broker shows elevated disk write IOPS and NIC utilization disproportionate to peers.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Increase offsets.topic.num.partitions from default 50 to 200+ at cluster bootstrap (immutable later); place __consumer_offsets log.dirs on dedicated NVMe separate from user-topic data; batch commits with commitAsync and longer auto.commit.interval.ms (e.g. 10-30s) to reduce commit rate; use manual commitSync only at checkpoint boundaries rather than per-batch; enable compression.type=producer on __consumer_offsets.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on kafka.server:BrokerTopicMetrics.MessagesInPerSec for topic=__consumer_offsets variance across partitions >3x, OFFSET_COMMIT request-latency-p99 >50ms, __consumer_offsets UnderReplicatedPartitions >0, and per-partition BytesInPerSec imbalance on the offsets topic.

bottlenecks.title: Log compaction lag causing bloated offset state and slow coordinator loads
bottlenecks.trigger: __consumer_offsets relies on log compaction to keep only the latest commit per (group, topic, partition) key. With ~3 groups × 1000 partitions = 3000 unique keys but commits arriving at 30k/sec, the dirty-to-clean ratio grows fast. Default log.cleaner.threads=1 and min.cleanable.dirty.ratio=0.5 mean compaction runs only when half the log is stale — by then a single partition can hold GBs of obsolete commits. On coordinator failover, the new coordinator must replay this entire log to rebuild group state.
bottlenecks.symptom: New coordinator takes 10-60s to load group metadata after failover (see GroupMetadataManager.group-load-time), consumers in affected groups stall with CoordinatorNotAvailable during this window, __consumer_offsets partitions grow to tens of GB despite only storing 3k unique keys, disk usage on coordinator brokers creeps upward steadily, log cleaner thread pegged at 100% CPU.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tune log.cleaner.threads=4-8 and min.cleanable.dirty.ratio=0.1 on __consumer_offsets so compaction runs aggressively; reduce segment.bytes for __consumer_offsets to 100MB (default 100MB, verify) so segments roll and become compactable faster; raise offsets.load.buffer.size to 16-32MB for faster coordinator loads; set offsets.retention.minutes down from 7-day default to 1-2 days to bound state for abandoned groups.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor kafka.log:LogCleanerManager.max-dirty-percent >60%, kafka.log:LogCleaner.cleaner-recopy-percent, __consumer_offsets partition size on disk >5GB (signals compaction falling behind), kafka.coordinator.group:GroupMetadataManager.group-load-time-max >5s, and log.cleaner.io-max-bytes-per-second saturation.

bottlenecks.title: Partition hotspotting from group-name hash skew
bottlenecks.trigger: Groups are mapped to __consumer_offsets partitions via hash(group.id) % 50. With only ~3 primary groups at 3x fanout but potentially dozens of sub-groups (microservices, replay jobs), and one dominant group (e.g. 'order-processor' with 100+ members committing every few seconds), 2-3 __consumer_offsets partitions absorb the majority of commit traffic while 40+ sit near idle. The coordinator broker leading those hot partitions handles the lion's share of OFFSET_COMMIT requests.
bottlenecks.symptom: One or two brokers show 5-10x higher __consumer_offsets BytesInPerSec than peers, correlated OFFSET_COMMIT latency spikes only on hot coordinators, heartbeat responses delayed on those brokers causing false session timeouts and cascading rebalances (see coord pre-build), uneven broker CPU distribution despite balanced user-topic traffic.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Initialize cluster with offsets.topic.num.partitions=200+ to spread the hash more finely; rename chronically hot groups (e.g. append a shard suffix) to rehash onto less-loaded partitions; run periodic preferred-leader-election on __consumer_offsets to rebalance leadership across all 50 brokers; for extreme hotspots, move the hot partitions to dedicated high-IO brokers via partition reassignment.
bottlenecks.detection: Track kafka.server:BrokerTopicMetrics.BytesInPerSec for topic=__consumer_offsets per-partition, alert when max/median ratio >3x; monitor kafka.coordinator.group:GroupMetadataManager.NumOffsets and NumGroups per broker for imbalance; correlate OFFSET_COMMIT request-latency-p99 per broker with specific __consumer_offsets partition ownership.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Offset Store exists for this queue For a Kafka-style queue where **3 consumer groups each read the full 1 GB/s stream independently**, each group needs to remember "I've processed up to offset 8,821,340,143 on partition orders-7." That bookmark has to survive consumer crashes, pod restarts, and deploys — otherwise a restarted consumer either replays the last 7 days of data (it's in the retention window!) or skips ahead and loses messages. The Offset Store is just a special Kafka topic (`__consumer_offsets`) that holds these bookmarks, one commit per `(group, topic, partition)` key. ## What happens without it Imagine consumer bookmarks lived in each consumer's local memory. A pod restart loses the bookmark; the consumer either restarts from offset 0 (replaying **86 TB/day** of data — your downstream database melts) or from "latest" (silently skipping every record produced during the outage — orders vanish). The operator sees either a thundering replay storm hammering brokers or quiet data loss discovered days later by a reconciliation job. Either way, the "3x fanout, durable queue" promise is broken. ## The number At **3M consumes/sec** (1M ingest × 3 fanout), committing per-record would be absurd — so consumers batch commits (~every 5s or every 100 records), landing around **30k commits/sec** across the cluster. Spread over the 50 default `__consumer_offsets` partitions, that's ~600 commits/sec/partition — trivial for Kafka's append-only log, which is already built for 100 MB/s/broker sustained writes. ## Trade-off Reusing Kafka's own log as the offset store avoids an external database dependency, but it means offset reads after a coordinator failover require replaying a compacted log — adding seconds to recovery.

operations.title: Produce a message (acks=all, replication factor 3)
operations.name: Produce a message (acks=all, replication factor 3)
operations.description: Producer sends a record to the partition leader; leader appends to its log, waits for ISR replication, then acks.

steps.title: Producer batches and selects partition
steps.action: Application calls producer.send(...). The record is keyed, assigned to a partition via murmur2(key) % num_partitions, and buffered in the accumulator for that partition.

steps.title: Bootstrap LB — bypassed after metadata cache
steps.action: Producer already has the metadata map from an earlier bootstrap call. This frame goes DIRECTLY to broker-12 (the leader of orders-7), bypassing the LB entirely.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Only hit on metadata refresh
# Otherwise: TCP connection producer → broker-12:9092 directly
steps.note: This is why LBs in Kafka-style systems are a boot-time concern, not a per-request concern.

steps.title: Leader broker (broker-12) receives PRODUCE
steps.action: Broker decompresses the batch enough to validate CRCs, then appends the serialized batch to the active log segment for partition orders-7.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# On broker-12 (leader of orders-7)
if not is_leader("orders-7"): return NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION
for batch in req.batches: validate_crc(batch) log = partitions["orders-7"].active_segment append_offset = log.leo # log-end-offset log.append(batch) # fsync per flush.messages, usually async log.leo += len(batch.records)
# Advance HW only after ISR replicates

steps.title: Append to segment on local SSD
steps.action: Bytes written to page cache; background flush thread fsyncs periodically. Index files updated sparsely (every 4KB of data).
steps.codeOrCommand:
pwrite(fd_log, batch_bytes, file_offset)
if (bytes_since_last_index >= 4096): pwrite(fd_idx, [offset → file_offset], idx_offset)

steps.title: Followers FETCH the new records
steps.action: broker-27 and broker-41 each have an open FETCH request to the leader (long-poll). The append wakes the long-poll and both followers receive the batch in parallel.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Follower loop on each replica
resp = fetch(leader=broker-12, partition="orders-7", offset=self.leo)
self.log.append(resp.batch)
self.leo = resp.base_offset + len(resp.records)
# Send FETCH again with updated offset
fetch(leader, "orders-7", offset=self.leo)

steps.title: Leader advances HW once min.insync.replicas ack
steps.action: Each follower's next FETCH reports its new LEO. When the ISR's min LEO reaches 8821340143 (i.e. at least 2 replicas including leader caught up), the leader advances the high-watermark and acks the producer.
steps.codeOrCommand: on_fetch_from_follower(f, reported_leo): follower_leo[f] = reported_leo insync = [leo for b, leo in follower_leo.items if in_isr(b)] insync.append(self.leo) new_hw = min(insync) if new_hw > self.hw: self.hw = new_hw for pending in acks_waiting[<new_hw]: pending.ack
steps.note: With min.insync.replicas=2, leader + 1 follower is enough to ack. RF=3 provides headroom.

steps.title: Producer receives offset and continues
steps.action: Send future resolves with the base offset; producer's idempotence sequence advances. Latency end-to-end ~5-15ms depending on replica geography.
steps.codeOrCommand: future.complete(RecordMetadata{topic:"orders", partition:7, offset:8821340000})

operations.title: Consume a message (fetch by offset)
operations.name: Consume a message (fetch by offset)
operations.description: Consumer polls the leader for new records, processes them, and commits the offset back to the coordinator.

steps.title: Consumer polls assigned partitions
steps.action: Consumer is assigned orders-7 (from earlier JoinGroup). It sends a FETCH request to the partition leader with its next expected offset.

steps.title: Leader serves FETCH from page cache
steps.action: Broker checks that the offset is ≤ HW (only committed records are visible), reads the byte range from the log via zero-copy sendfile, and returns up to max_bytes.
steps.codeOrCommand:
if req.offset > hw: // consumer ahead of committed return FetchResponse(records=, hw=hw) # empty, not error
file_pos = index_lookup(req.offset)
byte_count = min(file_size - file_pos, req.max_bytes, hw_byte_pos - file_pos)
sendfile(client_socket, log_fd, file_pos, byte_count) // zero-copy
steps.decision: Offset ≤ HW → serve records. If offset > HW the response is empty (consumer is up to date).

steps.title: Bytes streamed via sendfile
steps.action: Page cache → NIC directly; no copy into the JVM heap. This is why a single broker serves ~1 GB/s with modest CPU.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Linux system call
sendfile(out_fd=socket, in_fd=log_fd, offset=file_pos, count=byte_count)

steps.title: Consumer processes records
steps.action: Each record in the batch is passed to the application handler. Processing is sequential per-partition so ordering is preserved.
steps.codeOrCommand:
for r in resp.records: handle_order(r.value) # business logic
last_offset = resp.records[-1].offset // 8821340142

steps.title: Consumer commits offset
steps.action: After successful processing the consumer sends OFFSET_COMMIT to its group coordinator.

steps.title: Offset appended to __consumer_offsets
steps.action: Compacted topic append. Old commits for the same (group, topic, partition) key will be garbage-collected by log compaction later.
steps.codeOrCommand:
// Treated as a normal partition append internally
// __consumer_offsets-17: append commit record

steps.title: Consumer loops back to poll
steps.action: Immediately issues the next FETCH at offset 8821340143. Typical consumer lag target: <100ms.

operations.title: Leader failover (controller elects new leader)
operations.name: Leader failover (controller elects new leader)
operations.description: Broker-12 (leader of orders-7) crashes. Controller detects the heartbeat miss, removes it from ISR, picks a new leader from the remaining ISR, and propagates the change.

steps.title: Broker-12 stops heartbeating
steps.action: Broker-12 crashes (hardware failure / OOM / kill -9). Its session in the controller's heartbeat registry expires after session.timeout.ms (default 18s; KRaft is faster, ~1s).
steps.codeOrCommand:
// Broker-12: process gone
// Its heartbeat thread no longer pings the controller

steps.title: Controller detects failure, recomputes leadership
steps.action: Controller marks broker-12 as offline in its metadata. For every partition that broker-12 led, it picks the first live replica in the ISR as the new leader (Kafka's default is 'preferred replica → first live in ISR').
steps.codeOrCommand: on_broker_down(broker_id=12): for partition in partitions_led_by[12]: # [orders-7, orders-12, billing-3] isr = metadata.isr(partition) # [12, 27, 41] isr.remove(12) # [27, 41] new_leader = isr[0] # 27 metadata.set_leader(partition, new_leader) metadata.leader_epoch[partition] += 1 # fences stale writes # Fan out notifications: for b in live_brokers: send(b, LeaderAndIsrRequest, changes) for b in live_brokers: send(b, UpdateMetadataRequest, full_map)

steps.title: Broker-27 promoted to leader
steps.action: Broker-27 receives LeaderAndIsrRequest. It stops being a follower for orders-7 and begins serving PRODUCE / FETCH as the leader. Its current LEO becomes the new high-watermark (truncated if it was ahead of the old HW).
steps.codeOrCommand:
# On broker-27
make_leader("orders-7", epoch=43)
stop_follower_fetcher("orders-7")
start_produce_handler("orders-7")
# Truncate if needed so we don't expose unreplicated records
if self.leo > last_known_hw: truncate_to(last_known_hw)
self.hw = self.leo

steps.title: Broker-41 re-targets its follower fetcher
steps.action: Broker-41 (still a follower) sees the metadata update and now FETCHes from broker-27 instead of the dead broker-12.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# On broker-41
on_metadata_update("orders-7"): fetcher.retarget("orders-7", new_leader=27)

steps.title: In-flight producers retry with NOT_LEADER error
steps.action: Producers that were talking to broker-12 get a connection error or a NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION response. Their metadata refresh fetches the updated map and they reconnect to broker-27.
steps.codeOrCommand:
on_produce_error(NOT_LEADER): metadata.refresh // pulls new map new_leader = metadata.leader("orders-7") // 27 socket = connect(new_leader) socket.send(PRODUCE_REQUEST, batch, acks=-1) // retry
# Idempotence ensures no duplicates despite the retry
steps.decision: NOT_LEADER → refresh metadata → retry against new leader

steps.title: Consumers re-target fetches to broker-27
steps.action: Same pattern for consumers. FETCH returns NOT_LEADER; client refreshes metadata and re-issues FETCH against broker-27. Brief stall (hundreds of ms) but no data loss.
steps.codeOrCommand: on_fetch_error(NOT_LEADER): metadata.refresh next_fetch_target = metadata.leader("orders-7") // 27

steps.title: When broker-12 returns, it joins as a follower
steps.action: If broker-12 comes back, it discovers the metadata epoch has advanced and that orders-7 now has a different leader. It starts as a follower, truncates any uncommitted tail beyond the last-known HW, and catches up until its LEO re-enters the ISR.
steps.codeOrCommand: on_broker_rejoin(12): for partition_we_used_to_lead: current = metadata.leader_epoch(partition) if current > our_epoch: become_follower(partition, new_leader) truncate_to_known_safe_offset start_follower_fetcher
steps.note: Leadership does NOT automatically move back. A separate preferred-replica-election step can rebalance if desired.

tradeoffs.chosen: Per-partition FIFO only, no global order
tradeoffs.rationale: Global ordering would force a single writer and cap throughput; per-partition order is enough for 95% of workloads when keys are chosen well.
Simpler and faster than Paxos/Raft for the data path; acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2 gives no-data-loss on single-node failure at ~2-3x leader-only latency.

tradeoffs.chosen: Client-committed offsets stored back in Kafka
tradeoffs.rationale: Brokers stay stateless per consumer and replay is cheap; the cost is that at-least-once is the default and apps must handle duplicates.

tradeoffs.chosen: Append-only log with page cache, not a B-tree
tradeoffs.rationale: Sequential disk I/O is ~100x faster than random I/O and the page cache makes consumer reads free; the trade is no in-place update or per-key lookup.

tradeoffs.chosen: Dedicated controller (KRaft/ZK) separate from data brokers
tradeoffs.rationale: Isolates Raft quorum traffic from the firehose data path; failover decisions survive data-broker overload.
